Most cold calls die in the first ten seconds, and they die for the same reason. The caller starts talking about the product before the other person has agreed to listen. So the first thing you say is a question, and it is a question about permission. Hi, this is Flavio from Invent. Is this a bad time? Or, do you have two minutes? People almost never say no to two minutes. Then give the reason for the call in one sentence, and make it about them, not about you. I was calling because you work with mid-sized companies in Italy, and I think we can help your customers. Then the hook: one fact that makes them curious. And then do not ask for a meeting of one hour. Ask for something small. Would it be OK if I sent you one page, and we spoke for fifteen minutes next week? A small yes today is worth more than a big no.

I get about ten cold calls a week, and I stay on the line for maybe one of them. What makes the difference is not the accent and not the product. It is respect for my time. The good callers ask if it is a good moment, and if I say I am busy, they ask when they can call back, and they really call back at that time. The bad callers ignore my answer and keep talking. The other thing is the reason. If you say you were wondering if I had a few minutes, and then you tell me exactly why you chose my company, I listen. If it is clear that you are calling everybody on a list, I hang up. Last month a vendor from Brazil called me with a referral from a customer we share. He used the name in his first sentence. That was a warm call, not a cold one, and we have a meeting on Thursday.
